drafted_by: AI, requires clinician review before any real use.

questions.text: What is the main digestive problem: belly pain, nausea or vomiting, diarrhea, constipation, heartburn, trouble swallowing, or blood in stool?
questions.rationale: Clarifying the main complaint guides the next branch of the interview.

questions.text: Where is the belly pain, and does it move or spread anywhere, such as to your back or shoulder?
questions.rationale: Location and radiation narrow the differential.

questions.text: Did the pain start suddenly, how severe is it from 0 to 10, and is it constant or does it come in waves?
questions.rationale: Sudden severe pain suggests perforation, obstruction, ischemia, or colic.

questions.text: Is your belly hard, very tender to touch, or painful with any movement or bumps in the car?
questions.rationale: Peritoneal signs suggest perforation or peritonitis.

questions.text: Is the pain related to eating, such as better or worse after meals?
questions.rationale: Relationship to meals helps separate ulcer, gallbladder, and mesenteric causes.

questions.text: Do you have nausea or vomiting? How often, and what does the vomit look like?
questions.rationale: Vomiting pattern and content provide diagnostic clues.

questions.text: Have you vomited blood or material that looks like coffee grounds?
questions.rationale: This indicates upper GI bleeding requiring urgent evaluation.

questions.text: Have you had black, tarry, sticky stools?
questions.rationale: Melena indicates upper GI bleeding.

questions.text: Have you seen red blood in or on your stool, or on the toilet paper? How much?
questions.rationale: Hematochezia can be from hemorrhoids, colitis, diverticulosis, or colorectal cancer.

questions.text: Do you have diarrhea? How many loose stools a day, and for how long?
questions.rationale: Frequency and duration separate infectious, inflammatory, and functional causes.

questions.text: When was your last bowel movement, and are you still passing gas?
questions.rationale: Inability to pass stool or gas with distension and vomiting suggests obstruction.

questions.text: Is your belly swollen or bloated?
questions.rationale: Distension supports obstruction, ascites, or functional disease.

questions.text: Do you have heartburn or acid coming up, especially after meals or lying down?
questions.rationale: Reflux symptoms support GERD.

questions.text: Do you have trouble swallowing, food sticking, or unintended weight loss?
questions.rationale: Dysphagia with weight loss raises concern for esophageal or gastric cancer.

questions.text: Have your skin or eyes turned yellow, or has your urine become dark and stool pale?
questions.rationale: Jaundice suggests liver, gallbladder, or bile duct disease.

questions.text: Have you had fever or chills with the belly symptoms?
questions.rationale: Fever raises concern for appendicitis, cholangitis, diverticulitis, or infection.

questions.text: Are you very thirsty, dizzy on standing, or passing very little urine?
questions.rationale: These suggest significant dehydration.

questions.text: Did the symptoms start after a meal others also got sick from, restaurant food, or travel?
questions.rationale: Exposure history points to infectious gastroenteritis.

questions.text: Has your appetite changed or have you lost weight without trying?
questions.rationale: Unintended weight loss raises concern for malignancy or inflammatory disease.

questions.text: Do you take NSAIDs like ibuprofen or aspirin, or drink alcohol regularly?
questions.rationale: NSAIDs and alcohol cause gastritis, ulcers, and liver and pancreatic disease.

questions.text: Have you started antibiotics or any other new medicines?
questions.rationale: Medications are a common cause of GI symptoms including C. difficile risk after antibiotics.

questions.text: Do you have a history of ulcers, gallstones, IBD, IBS, celiac disease, or abdominal surgery?
questions.rationale: Past history shapes the likely cause and risk of obstruction or recurrence.

questions.text: Does anyone in your family have colon cancer, IBD, or celiac disease?
questions.rationale: Family history affects risk and workup urgency.

questions.text: Is pregnancy possible right now?
questions.rationale: Pregnancy changes the differential and imaging choices, including ectopic pregnancy.

questions.text: What is the main thing you are worried this could be?
questions.rationale: Understanding the patient's concern guides reassurance and follow-up questions.

red_flags.label: Vomiting blood or black stools
red_flags.detection_instructions: Does the patient report vomiting blood or coffee-ground material, or black tarry stools?

red_flags.label: Significant rectal bleeding
red_flags.detection_instructions: Does the patient report large amounts of red blood from the rectum, or bleeding with lightheadedness?

red_flags.label: Sudden severe abdominal pain or rigid abdomen
red_flags.detection_instructions: Does the patient describe sudden severe belly pain, a hard tender belly, or pain with any movement?

red_flags.label: Possible bowel obstruction
red_flags.detection_instructions: Does the patient report persistent vomiting with a swollen belly and no stool or gas passing?

red_flags.label: Jaundice with fever
red_flags.detection_instructions: Does the patient report yellow skin or eyes together with fever, chills, or right upper abdominal pain?

red_flags.label: Signs of significant dehydration
red_flags.detection_instructions: Does the patient report severe thirst, dizziness on standing, or very little urine?

red_flags.label: Trouble swallowing with weight loss
red_flags.detection_instructions: Does the patient report progressive difficulty swallowing with unintended weight loss?
